opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the way I understand it is that population-level screening is really a problem of scale and consistency. You have millions of mammograms being read every year, and the overwhelming majority of them are normal. Radiologists are extraordinarily skilled, but they're human. Fatigue sets in, there's variability between readers, and in many places there simply aren't enough trained breast radiologists to meet the demand. So the opportunity for AI isn't to replace the radiologist. It's to act as a kind of second set of eyes, or as a triage layer that helps decide where expert attention is most needed.

For example, in programs that use double reading, which is common in parts of Europe, an AI system can stand in as one of the two readers. That frees up specialist time without lowering the standard of care. In other settings, the AI might flag the cases it considers highest risk so they get looked at first, or identify the very clearly normal studies so radiologists can spend more of their energy on the ambiguous ones.

That said, I'm cautious about how we talk about this. A model that performs well on a curated dataset from one hospital doesn't automatically perform well across a whole population. Breast density varies, imaging equipment varies, and the demographics of who gets screened vary. If the training data underrepresents certain groups, you can end up with a tool that works well for some women and less well for others, and at the population level that becomes an equity problem. So for me, the real work is in prospective validation, careful monitoring after deployment, and thinking hard about how the tool fits into the clinical workflow. The algorithm is just one piece. How people use it, and whether it actually improves outcomes like earlier detection and fewer unnecessary recalls, is what really matters.

r002.rationale: The response describes AI flagging high-risk cases for earlier review, but does not say it flags cases warranting further screening.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, screening is really a problem of scale, and that's where AI tools actually make sense. In a mammography program you're looking at enormous volumes of images where the vast majority are normal, and radiologists are spending most of their time confirming that nothing is there. An algorithm that can reliably triage the clearly normal cases, or flag the ones that deserve a second look, doesn't replace the radiologist. It changes where their attention goes.

But I'd push back on the idea that the role is just "find more cancers." At a population level, the question is whether you're finding the cancers that matter, at the right time, without driving up false positives and unnecessary biopsies. A tool that boosts sensitivity but also doubles recalls is not a win for a screening program. So the metrics we care about are things like interval cancer rates, recall rates, and whether the tool performs consistently across different scanners, sites, and populations, including people with dense breasts who are historically underserved by mammography.

The other piece I think about a lot is that these models learn from the data they're given, and screening data carries all the biases of who got screened and who got diagnosed. If you deploy a model trained in one health system into another with a different population, you need to validate it there, not assume it transfers. Prospective evaluation in the actual workflow matters more than retrospective accuracy numbers.

So in short: I see AI as a way to make screening more efficient and potentially more equitable, but only if it's evaluated as a system-level intervention rather than as a standalone image classifier.

r001.rationale: The response says the vast majority of mammography images in screening are normal, communicating that only a small proportion of screened cases have cancer.

r002.rationale: It describes AI as flagging cases that deserve a second look, equivalent to identifying cases for further screening.

astra-6.text:
I think of AI as a tool to support the entire screening pathway. Reading a mammogram is one part of that, but at a population level, we also have to ask: Who is being screened? Who is being missed? And who gets timely follow-up when something concerning is found?

AI could help identify suspicious findings, support radiologists, and potentially help us tailor screening to a person’s risk. But the question is whether those tools actually improve outcomes. Do we catch clinically important cancers earlier? Do we reduce unnecessary testing? And do those benefits extend across the population, rather than just to people who already have good access to care?

So I see real potential, but we need to evaluate these systems within the healthcare settings where they’ll be used. A strong result on a dataset is a starting point; the goal is better care for the people being screened.

r002.rationale: It says AI could identify suspicious findings and support radiologists, but does not clearly say AI flags cases that warrant further screening.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the role is to help us make screening more effective across the whole population. That means looking beyond whether an AI system can identify a cancer on a mammogram. Does it help us catch cancers earlier? Can it reduce unnecessary callbacks and biopsies? And does it work well for people across different ages, breast densities, and communities?

There’s also an opportunity to use AI to better understand risk, so we can move toward screening that’s more tailored to the individual. But those tools need to be evaluated carefully in real screening programs. A strong result on a retrospective dataset doesn’t automatically translate into better outcomes for patients.

For me, AI should support the people delivering care, with clear accountability and ongoing monitoring. The goal is better, more equitable screening—not simply adding another technology.

r001.rationale: The response discusses population screening but does not state that only a small proportion of screened women have cancer.

r002.rationale: It mentions identifying cancer and reducing callbacks, but does not characterize AI as flagging cases that warrant further screening.
